one_paragraph_summary: Continuing his post-pardon dialogue with Joseph Estrada -- who asked, 'I appointed six justices, yet none of them voted for me. Why?' -- Panganiban delivers a meditation on judicial independence as the primus inter pares of the four constitutional attributes required of judges (competence, integrity, probity, independence). Independence is most crucial because the judiciary is mandated to check the executive; those who don the black robe undergo a transformation, become different persons, forfeit past activities, relatives, and friends -- 'especially the president who appointed them' -- and devote their full time and attention to the exclusive and reclusive world of decision-making. He explains the doctrinal architecture of Estrada vs Desierto (March 3, 2001): by then the Senate and House had already passed separate resolutions supporting Arroyo's ascent, and those resolutions were beyond judicial review as political questions delegated to the legislative branch; the international community had also recognized her government. He cites the separate opinion of Justice Angelina Sandoval-Gutierrez -- Estrada's last appointee, who had taken office just a month before Edsa 2 -- to powerful effect: 'this Court has to declare as a fact what in fact exists. Respondent Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo is the de jure President of the Republic of the Philippines.' He raises the counterfactual: had the Court not affirmed her legitimacy, Arroyo (then controlling the military and police) would have been tempted to set aside the Constitution and establish a revolutionary government, altering Philippine history. Estrada, he notes, is not the first or the last president to lament appointee 'ingratitude' -- even P-Noy has expressed dismay over some of his own appointees. He cites Justice Alfredo Benjamin Caguioa's model JBC reply on how he would decide critical cases involving P-Noy ('my former boss, school buddy and close friend'): 'My impartiality and probity as a judge would not be compromised by utang na loob.' He notes Arroyo herself was probably disappointed by Panganiban Court decisions striking down (1) her EO 464 barring Cabinet from Senate testimony, (2) her calibrated preemptive response against rallies, (3) her declaration of a state of national emergency, and (4) her people's initiative to shift to parliamentary form. The moral lesson: presidents should expect a cutting of umbilical ties when jurists enter the SC's hallowed doors and should be happy, or at least consoled, that their appointees lived up to fiat justitia ruat caelum (do justice though the heavens may fall). When Estrada follows up -- 'If they could not side with me, why did they not just inhibit like you?' -- Panganiban explains the Rules of Court grounds for compulsory disqualification (pecuniary interest, kinship within sixth degree, prior involvement) and voluntary inhibition (sound discretion, including personal bias or prejudice under the Code of Judicial Conduct). None of those applied to the six Estrada appointees; thus they did not inhibit. In his own case, however, Panganiban voluntarily inhibited because counsel Rene A. V. Saguisag filed a formal petition alleging he and CJ Davide may have prejudged the cause. He replied to the Court that 'although petitioner had not proven any legal ground for his request, I was nonetheless voluntarily inhibiting for two reasons: (1) to hold myself above petitioner's reproach and suspicion and (2) to deprive him or anyone else of any excuse to cast any doubt on the integrity of these proceedings and of the decision that this Court may render.' Aside from the totality test ratio decidendi, separate opinions also discussed Estrada's permanent disability and abandonment as alternative justifications for Arroyo's ascent.
